blocks.text: Chapter 1: The Price of Being a Good Wife
My name is Clara Morales, and for seven years, I believed that saving my marriage was my responsibility alone.
Javier Rivas had once been charming. He brought me flowers, remembered every little thing I liked, and promised that we would build a life where neither of us would ever feel alone.

When his consulting business began attracting wealthy clients, his patience disappeared. He started criticizing my clothes, mocking my modest background, and treating every disagreement as a personal insult.
“Men like Javier need women who understand their position in society,” she often told me. “Not women who make them feel guilty for earning money.”
I worked as a financial compliance consultant. My job involved examining transactions, identifying irregularities, and tracing money that people hoped would remain hidden.
Ironically, Javier never took my profession seriously.
He had no idea how much I understood about the business world he worshipped.
Our marriage had been deteriorating for months when Mercedes announced that we would celebrate Javier’s latest business achievement at a prestigious restaurant in central Madrid.
“It’s an important evening,” she said over the phone. “Don’t embarrass my son.”
Instead, I put on a simple white dress and arrived at the restaurant at eight o’clock.
Mercedes was already seated, wearing diamonds that flashed beneath the crystal chandeliers.
“You could have worn something more appropriate,” he muttered.
That was when the evening began to unravel.
Mercedes ordered champagne before anyone had even opened the menu.
Then came oysters, lobster, imported caviar, premium steaks, and several bottles of wine.
Whenever I questioned another extravagant order, she waved her hand dismissively.
“It’s a celebration, Clara. Try not to be so provincial.”
“Must you always make everything uncomfortable?”
I looked toward the other diners. Several had noticed the tension, but nobody intervened.
“Javier tells me you’ve been asking questions about his business accounts.”
“I asked why money was being transferred from our joint savings account into an unfamiliar company.”
“That money belongs to my son,” she snapped.
“Then perhaps we shouldn’t be spending nearly five thousand euros here.”
Mercedes gave a short, contemptuous laugh.
“Listen to her. She wants to enjoy the benefits of being married to a successful man but refuses to support him when it matters.”
When the bill arrived, he didn’t even glance at it. He pushed it directly toward me.
“You invited me to dinner. You and your mother chose everything. Why should I pay for all of it?”
His chair scraped against the floor as he stood.
“Pay the bill, Clara, or our marriage ends tonight.”
I felt something inside me settle into a frightening calm.
For years, I had mistaken his anger for strength and my silence for love.
He snatched his glass and threw the wine directly into my face.
The liquid struck my forehead and ran down my cheeks, soaking my dress.
I reached for a napkin, wiped my face, and took out my phone.
Chapter 3: The Call That Changed Everything
I gave the restaurant’s address and explained that my husband had thrown wine at me during an argument and was threatening me.
I asked for assistance and made it clear that I was afraid the situation might escalate.
Javier laughed loudly enough for nearby tables to hear.
“She’s calling the police because of wine! Do you understand how ridiculous that sounds?”
Instead, I looked toward the restaurant manager, who had been watching the confrontation from several meters away.
He approached our table with two security employees.
“Señor Rivas,” he said, “please step away from your wife.”
“Yes,” Andrés replied. “And that is precisely why we need you to remain here.”
For the first time that evening, Javier seemed uncertain.
“Señora Morales, the documents you requested have arrived. We have kept them secure.”
“The ones concerning the company you used to move money from our joint account.”
“No,” I replied. “I’ve been protecting myself.”
The restaurant staff guided us into separate areas while we waited for the authorities.
Javier attempted to leave, but security asked him to remain until the officers arrived.
He began shouting about lawyers, reputations, and the consequences of embarrassing a prominent businessman.
When the officers arrived, I gave my account of what had happened. I explained that Javier had thrown wine at me and threatened me after I refused to pay.
The officers spoke to witnesses and restaurant staff, then handled the situation according to the circumstances.
Javier’s confidence began to crumble when two diners volunteered what they had seen.
“This is a private family disagreement!”
“Ma’am, an incident in a public restaurant is not automatically a private matter simply because the people involved are married.”
The documents Andrés had mentioned would expose something far more damaging.
